title: The Passenger Manifest
subtitle: Welcome to the Records Room
historicalNote: This chapter uses fictional training passengers inspired by the setting of RMS Titanic. These records are NOT genuine historical passenger records.

lessons.title: Meet the Database
lessons.objective: Learn what a table, a row, and a column are.
lessons.story: The archive has received a small practice ledger of passenger records. Before beginning your research, inspect how its information is organized.
lessons.explanation: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is how you ask a database questions. Think of the passengers table as a spreadsheet: each row is one passenger record, and each column holds one kind of information (such as a name or age). A query asks the database to show you particular information. You can inspect records safely: SELECT only reads them.
lessons.task: Now change the example: show ALL columns from the passengers table, but return FIVE rows instead of two.
hints: SELECT * requests every column; LIMIT 5 restricts the sample.
lessons.solutionExplanation: SELECT * retrieves every column; FROM specifies the table; LIMIT 5 keeps the result short.

keyTerms.meaning: Start a question to the database. It tells SQL which columns to show.
An asterisk means ALL columns in this table—not multiplication here, and not a request for a certain number of rows.
Introduces the source table. FROM passengers means 'look in the passengers table'.
Sets the maximum number of rows shown. LIMIT 2 gives you at most two passenger records.
The semicolon marks the end of a SQL statement. Many editors accept a single query without it, but using it is a helpful habit.

example.context: The archivist wants a quick look at two records, including every column they contain.
walkthrough: SELECT begins the request.
* tells the database to return every column (name, age, ticket and the others).
FROM passengers identifies the table holding the records.
LIMIT 2 asks for just two rows; ; finishes the statement.
Press Run example to see the real database response. Then change the number for your mission.
example.takeaway: SQL isn't case-sensitive for these keywords. The query displays at most two rows; without ORDER BY, the database does not guarantee which two.

lessons.title: Your First Query
lessons.objective: Select a single column using SELECT and FROM.
lessons.story: The curator is preparing an index of names. She needs only the names, not every detail in the ledger.
lessons.explanation: Now that you know SELECT and FROM, you can choose a single column instead of displaying everything with *. Write the column's exact name after SELECT. The Database Explorer lists the valid column names. Column names like age and name are data fields, not SQL keywords.
lessons.task: Your turn: the archivist needs a list of passenger NAMES only. Return the name column for every record, with no extra columns.
hints: The column is called name, without an s.
lessons.solutionExplanation: SELECT name returns just the name column, without extra passenger details.

keyTerms.meaning: Ask for only the age column instead of every column.
Read those ages from the passengers table.
A different column you will need in the task. Use the exact spelling—there is no column called names.

example.context: The archivist wants a list of passenger ages. No names or ticket information are needed.
walkthrough: After SELECT, write the exact column you want: age.
FROM passengers chooses the table.
There is no LIMIT, so the query requests every record. Only the age column appears.
The semicolon completes the statement.
example.takeaway: Use SELECT * to inspect everything, but select a named column when your question needs only that information.

lessons.title: Passenger Profiles
lessons.story: The archive's researcher wants to compare ages and names while reviewing the ledger.
lessons.explanation: You can request several columns at the same time. Write their names after SELECT, separated by commas. The result follows the left-to-right order in your SELECT list. The comma separates columns; it does not filter rows.
lessons.task: Now retrieve TWO fields for each passenger: name followed by age. Return all passengers.
hints: Separate the field names with a comma.
Try SELECT name, age FROM passengers;
lessons.solutionExplanation: SELECT name, age produces a two-column result, with one row per passenger.

keyTerms.meaning: A comma separates column names. It means 'also show this column'.
Two requested columns appear in the resulting table in that order.
SELECT name, age and SELECT age, name contain the same information but display columns in different positions.

example.context: The archive wants to compare a passenger's class with the fare printed on their ticket.
walkthrough: Start with SELECT and list passenger_class followed by ticket_fare.
Put a comma between the two names.
Use FROM passengers to find the records.
LIMIT 3 shows a small sample so you can check the output.
example.takeaway: You can add another column by adding a comma and its name. Only include fields relevant to the question.

lessons.title: A Shorter Register
lessons.objective: Use LIMIT to request a small sample.
lessons.story: The chief archivist is printing a short sample for a colleague. Space on the page is limited.
lessons.explanation: When a table has many records, you may want just a sample. LIMIT N requests at most N rows. Put it after FROM. A row is a whole passenger record; a column is one attribute. LIMIT does not control which columns are returned.
lessons.task: Prepare a five-row sample with exactly two columns: name and passenger_class. Use LIMIT to return no more than five records.
lessons.referenceSql: SELECT name, passenger_class FROM passengers LIMIT 5;
lessons.solutionExplanation: LIMIT 5 keeps only the first five records in the practice table's present order.

keyTerms.meaning: Returns no more than two rows, even if the table has many more.
Your task needs a five-row sample. Write LIMIT after FROM.
A keyword you will learn later. Without it, SQL does not promise any meaningful or stable row order.

example.context: A colleague needs a short sample containing names and ages.
walkthrough: Select exactly the requested columns, separated by a comma.
Choose the passengers table using FROM.
Add LIMIT 2 at the end to cap the result to two rows.
Run the example, then change both the columns and row limit for your task.
example.takeaway: LIMIT is useful for exploring data. It does not necessarily return the oldest, first-booked, or historically earliest passengers.

lessons.title: Your First Assignment
lessons.objective: Combine selecting multiple fields and limiting results.
lessons.story: The records supervisor requests a ten-entry summary showing each passenger's identifier, name, and ticket price. This is your first independent archive assignment.
lessons.explanation: A business request often combines things you already know. Translate it into three questions: Which columns are needed? Which table contains them? How many rows should be displayed? SQL keywords are instructions; column names refer to data. Build the query in order: SELECT columns, FROM table, optional LIMIT, and finally a semicolon.
lessons.task: Independent assignment: return exactly the columns passenger_id, name and ticket_fare (in that order) from passengers, showing no more than ten rows. Avoid extra columns.
lessons.referenceSql: SELECT passenger_id, name, ticket_fare FROM passengers LIMIT 10;
hints: The three requested column names are shown in the explorer.
Separate the columns with commas and use the passengers table.
lessons.solutionExplanation: You combined multiple columns, a source table, and a row limit to satisfy a practical data request.

keyTerms.meaning: Choose the requested information, separating the names with commas.
Use the training passenger records as your data source.
Produce no more than ten passenger records for the supervisor.
Two hyphens start a comment: the database ignores the rest of that line. Comments can remind you what a query is for.

example.context: A colleague requests a short list of names and ages from four practice records.
example.sql:
-- Example archive request
SELECT name, age
FROM passengers
LIMIT 4;
walkthrough: Ignore the comment line; it only explains the purpose to a human.
Identify the two needed columns and list them after SELECT.
Read the data FROM passengers.
Limit the output to four rows. Your assignment will ask for different fields and a different row count.
example.takeaway: You can solve a new task by translating the request into the SQL structure you have already practiced.
